items.rationale: The program fixes the steps and their order; the model only writes the answer inside one step. When the code owns the control flow, it is a workflow. Answering 'the model' because a model is called shows M7.

The difference is who owns the control flow: in a workflow, code fixes the path; in an agent, the model decides the next step and which tool to use. Workflows can use models (a) and tools (b), and step count (c) does not separate them.
Booking is the same sequence every time, so code can fix it: cheaper, faster and easier to test. The other three depend on what is found along the way, which is where an agent's flexibility pays off.
Because the workflow's path is fixed, its cost is predictable: 1,200 / 3 = 400 requests. An agent's number of calls varies with each request, so it cannot be budgeted this exactly.

Routing is still a workflow: the code defines every path in advance and the model only chooses among them. A model making a decision does not make the system an agent; an agent decides its own steps, not just a branch.

An agent earns its extra cost when the path cannot be known ahead, because each step depends on earlier results. Frequency (b) and a need for accuracy (d) say nothing about whether the path is fixed, and several steps (c) can still be a fixed sequence that code runs.
